topic: Research gang violence in Mexico and its outlook in 2025, as if we are at the end of 2024 heading into 2025.
initial_thesis: Mexico’s Crackdown Is Fueling a Cartel Rebalance
final_thesis: Sharpen: ACLED data for 2024 indicates Mexico’s security push did not produce a CJNG-led national surge but redistributed violence toward logistics corridors and select urban nodes, with Sinaloa-aligned activity expanding most. Three pivots define the year: (1) a pronounced shift to corridor hot spots—Sinaloa/Culiacán and adjacent municipalities; the southern border (Chiapas–Tabasco) with Tabasco’s retail/energy corridor and Chiapas border towns; and industrial-urban hubs (Nuevo León, Guanajuato, CDMX)—while prior epicenters like Zacatecas and Tamaulipas contracted; (2) a marked rise in cartel–state confrontations (+45% YoY) concentrated in Michoacán, Chiapas, Guerrero, and a single-month spike in Zacatecas, paired with late-2024 enforcement surges (arrests and disrupted weapons use up in Q4); and (3) tactical emphasis on coordinated disruption (arson, roadblocks, retail attacks) with low per-event lethality, alongside persistently high violence against civilians and selective high-fatality outliers. Actor balance shows CJNG dominant but stable in share and concentrated in Michoacán/Chiapas, while Sinaloa gains share and salience (Culiacán as the standout municipal hotspot). Entering 2025, expect concentrated flashpoints along Pacific logistics and the southern border, periodic disruption waves affecting mobility and commerce, continued pressure on state forces in Michoacán/Chiapas, and opportunistic incursions into urban-industrial belts—against a backdrop of limited technological escalation (drones/IEDs still marginal) and persistent civilian intimidation despite macro socioeconomic gains.

judgments.finding: "Following the violent 2024 election season, Mexico introduced significant reforms aimed at disrupting gang operations and reducing their societal grip. These efforts included overhauling law enforcement, granting more autonomy to judicial bodies, and enhancing protections for vulnerable political candidates and community leaders[8]. Financial investigations and asset seizures were also prioritized to dismantle the economic power of organized crime networks, alongside stronger federal-local collaboration to address regional complexities[9]. While these measures are expected to play a key role in curbing gang violence and restoring public trust, the adaptability of criminal groups to these changes leaves the long-term impact uncertain as we move into 2025[9]."
judgments.rationale: The summary describes broad post-2024 reforms and notes uncertain long-term impact due to cartel adaptability. This neither substantiates nor contradicts specific claims about a CJNG-led surge or corridor-specific redistribution, but it adds a caveat that reforms may not tame conflict due to adaptation.
